solution:
The set of points \((x, y)\) equidistant from two points is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. Equating the squared distances from \((a+b,\ b-a)\) and \((a-b,\ a+b)\):
\[(x-(a+b))^2+(y-(b-a))^2=(x-(a-b))^2+(y-(a+b))^2.\]
The \(x^2\) and \(y^2\) terms cancel, and since \((a+b)^2+(b-a)^2=(a-b)^2+(a+b)^2\) the constants cancel too, leaving
\[-2(a+b)x-2(b-a)y=-2(a-b)x-2(a+b)y.\]
Thus \((a+b-a+b)x+(b-a-a-b)y=0\), i.e. \(2bx-2ay=0\), so \(bx-ay=0\). Hence (B).
The line through \((1, 0)\) and \((0, 1)\) is \(x + y = 1\). For \((x, 8)\) to be collinear it must satisfy this: \(x + 8 = 1\), so \(x = -7\). Hence (D).

Take \((0, 0)\) as one vertex with adjacent sides \(\vec{u}=(7, 2)\) and \(\vec{v}=(5, 9)\); the fourth vertex \((12, 11)=\vec{u}+\vec{v}\) confirms a parallelogram. Area \(=|7\cdot 9-2\cdot 5|=|63-10|=53.\) Hence (D).

\(A\) and \(B\) trisect \(PQ\). \(A=P+\tfrac{1}{3}(Q-P)=(1, 2)+\tfrac{1}{3}(-5, -10)=\left(-\tfrac{2}{3}, -\tfrac{4}{3}\right);\) \(B=P+\tfrac{2}{3}(Q-P)=\left(-\tfrac{7}{3}, -\tfrac{14}{3}\right).\) Midpoint of \(AB=\left(\tfrac{-2/3-7/3}{2}, \tfrac{-4/3-14/3}{2}\right)=\left(-\tfrac{3}{2}, -3\right).\) Hence (B).

The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. Midpoint of the given diagonal \((-1, 0)\)-\((-2, 1)\) is \(\left(-\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\right).\) The other diagonal joins \((-6, 5)\) and the unknown vertex \((x, y)\), with the same midpoint: \(\tfrac{-6+x}{2}=-\tfrac{3}{2}\Rightarrow x=3;\ \tfrac{5+y}{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\Rightarrow y=-4.\) Fourth vertex \((3, -4)\). Hence (C).

The centroid \(G\) divides the segment from the circumcentre \(O\) to the orthocentre \(H\) in the ratio \(OG : GH = 1 : 2\), so \(G=O+\tfrac{1}{3}(H-O).\) \(G=(5, 5)+\tfrac{1}{3}((2, 2)-(5, 5))=(5, 5)+\tfrac{1}{3}(-3, -3)=(4, 4).\) Hence (D).
The locus is the perpendicular bisector of \((1, 1)\)-\((3, 3)\). Midpoint \((2, 2)\); the segment has slope \(1\), so the bisector has slope \(-1\): \(y-2=-(x-2)\), i.e. \(x+y=4.\) Hence (B).
\(OA\) is split into \(1+2+3=6\) equal parts. \(P\) is at \(\tfrac{1}{6}\) of \(64\): \(P=\left(\tfrac{64}{6}, 0\right)=\left(\tfrac{32}{3}, 0\right).\) Hence (A).

If \(\left(2, \tfrac{2}{3}\right)\) is the midpoint of the vertex \((3, 3)\) and \(B\), then \(B=(2\cdot 2-3,\ 2\cdot\tfrac{2}{3}-3)=\left(1, -\tfrac{5}{3}\right).\) Similarly \(C=(2\cdot 4-3,\ 2\cdot\tfrac{3}{2}-3)=(5, 0).\) Centroid \(=\left(\tfrac{3+1+5}{3}, \tfrac{3-5/3+0}{3}\right)=\left(3, \tfrac{4}{9}\right).\) Hence (C).

The point dividing \((1, 1)\)-\((2, 4)\) in \(3 : 2\) is \(\left(\tfrac{3\cdot 2+2\cdot 1}{5}, \tfrac{3\cdot 4+2\cdot 1}{5}\right)=\left(\tfrac{8}{5}, \tfrac{14}{5}\right).\) Then \(k=2x+y=\tfrac{16}{5}+\tfrac{14}{5}=\tfrac{30}{5}=6.\) Hence (A).

The centroid of a triangle coincides with the centroid of the triangle formed by the midpoints of its sides. So centroid \(=\left(\tfrac{11+2+2}{3}, \tfrac{9+1-1}{3}\right)=\left(\tfrac{15}{3}, \tfrac{9}{3}\right)=(5, 3).\) Hence (A).
Both points have \(x=-1\), so the distance is \(|a-(-4a)|=|5a|.\) Setting \(|5a|=10\) gives \(a=\pm 2.\) Hence (B).

Take vectors from the first vertex. \(P_2 - P_1 = \big((a+1)(a+2) - a(a+1),\ 1\big) = (2a+2,\ 1)\) and \(P_3 - P_1 = \big((a+2)(a+3) - a(a+1),\ 2\big) = (4a+6,\ 2)\). Area \(= \frac{1}{2}\,\lvert (2a+2)(2) - (4a+6)(1) \rvert = \frac{1}{2}\,\lvert 4a+4 - 4a-6 \rvert = \frac{1}{2}(2) = 1\). The area is 1 for every value of a. Answer: (B).
In rectangle \(ABCD\), \(AB=|2-(-1)|=3\) (horizontal) and \(AD=|4-0|=4\) (vertical), so \(C=B+(D-A)=(2, 4).\) Diagonal \(AC=\sqrt{(2-(-1))^2+(4-0)^2}=\sqrt{9+16}=5.\) Hence (D).

Squared distance \(=a^2(\cos\alpha-\cos\beta)^2+a^2(\sin\alpha-\sin\beta)^2=a^2\big(2-2\cos(\alpha-\beta)\big)=4a^2\sin^2\!\left(\tfrac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\right).\) Taking the root, distance \(=2\left|a\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\right)\right|.\) Hence (B).

The side joining \((0, 1)\) and \((0, -1)\) has length \(2\). For an equilateral triangle the distance from \((x, 0)\) to each must be \(2\): \(x^2+1=4\Rightarrow x^2=3\Rightarrow x=\pm\sqrt{3}.\) So \(x=\sqrt{3}, -\sqrt{3}.\) Hence (B).

Distance between \((2, 3)\) and \((-5, 2)\) is \(\sqrt{49+1}=\sqrt{50}.\) Distance between \((x, 2)\) and \((1, 3)\) is \(\sqrt{(x-1)^2+1}.\) Equating squares: \((x-1)^2=49\Rightarrow x-1=\pm 7\Rightarrow x=8\) or \(x=-6.\) Hence (A).

Let the circumcentre be \((h, k)\). Equidistance from \((4, 0)\) and \((30, 0)\) gives \((h-4)^2=(h-30)^2\Rightarrow h=17.\) The keyed answer \((17, 17)\) matches this \(x\)-coordinate uniquely among the options. (Note: equidistance from \((0, 3)\) gives \(k=21.5\), so the printed \(y\)-value is inconsistent.) Hence (D).

With \(AC\) the hypotenuse the right angle is at \(B(1, 1)\). Side \(BC\) (to \((2, 1)\)) is horizontal of length \(1\), so \(BA\) must be vertical, giving \(A=(1, k)\) with \(h=1\). Area \(=\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot BC\cdot BA=\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot|k-1|=1\Rightarrow|k-1|=2\Rightarrow k=3\) or \(k=-1.\) So \(\{-1, 3\}.\) Hence (A).

With common ratio \(r\): \(x_2=x_1r,\ x_3=x_1r^2\) and \(y_2=y_1r,\ y_3=y_1r^2.\) Each point \((x_1r^k, y_1r^k)\) lies on the line \(y=\tfrac{y_1}{x_1}x\), so the three points are collinear. Hence (D).
All four points satisfy \(y=\tfrac{b}{a}x\): \((-a, -b)\), \((a, b)\), \((0, 0)\) clearly, and for \((a^2, ab)\), \(\tfrac{b}{a}\cdot a^2=ab.\) So they are always collinear. Hence (A).
The line through \((a, b)\) and \((-a, -b)\) passes through the origin with slope \(\tfrac{b}{a}\): \(y=\tfrac{b}{a}x.\) Testing \((a^2, ab)\): \(\tfrac{b}{a}\cdot a^2=ab,\) which holds. Hence (C).

\(D=\) midpoint of \(BC=\left(\tfrac{a}{2}, 0\right),\) so median \(AD\) has slope \(\dfrac{0-b}{a/2-0}=-\dfrac{2b}{a}.\) \(E=\) midpoint of \(AC=\left(\tfrac{a}{2}, \tfrac{b}{2}\right),\) so median \(BE\) has slope \(\dfrac{b/2}{a/2}=\dfrac{b}{a}.\) Perpendicularity: \(\left(-\tfrac{2b}{a}\right)\!\left(\tfrac{b}{a}\right)=-1\Rightarrow a^2=2b^2\Rightarrow a=\pm\sqrt{2}\,b.\) Hence (D).

Line through \(\left(0, \tfrac{8}{3}\right)\) and \((1, 3)\) has slope \(\dfrac{3-8/3}{1}=\tfrac{1}{3}\), giving \(y=\tfrac{1}{3}x+\tfrac{8}{3}.\) At \(x=82\): \(\tfrac{82}{3}+\tfrac{8}{3}=\tfrac{90}{3}=30,\) which matches \((82, 30).\) So the points lie on a straight line. Hence (D).
If \(3, x_1, x_2\) and \(4, y_1, y_2\) are each in A.P., then \(B\) and \(C\) advance by equal coordinate increments from \(A\), so all three lie on one line. Hence (B), collinear.
Slope \(=\dfrac{a-4}{-2-3}=\dfrac{a-4}{-5}.\) Setting this equal to \(-\tfrac{2}{5}\): \(\dfrac{a-4}{-5}=-\tfrac{2}{5}\Rightarrow a-4=2\Rightarrow a=6.\) Hence (A).
A line that never meets the x-axis is parallel to it (horizontal), and a horizontal line has slope \(0.\) Hence (D).

Median \(PM\) to the midpoint \(M=\left(\tfrac{a}{2}, 0\right)\) of \(QR\) has slope \(\dfrac{0-b}{a/2}=-\dfrac{2b}{a}.\) Median \(QN\) to the midpoint \(N=\left(\tfrac{a}{2}, \tfrac{b}{2}\right)\) of \(PR\) has slope \(\dfrac{b/2}{a/2}=\dfrac{b}{a}.\) Perpendicularity: \(-\tfrac{2b}{a}\cdot\tfrac{b}{a}=-1\Rightarrow a^2=2b^2.\) Hence (C).
The line through \((3q, 0)\) and \((0, 3p)\) is \(\dfrac{x}{3q}+\dfrac{y}{3p}=1.\) For \((1, 1)\) on it: \(\dfrac{1}{3q}+\dfrac{1}{3p}=1\Rightarrow\dfrac{1}{p}+\dfrac{1}{q}=3.\) Hence (C).
If \(P(3,5)\) bisects the intercept, the axis intercepts are \((6,0)\) and \((0,10)\). Line: \(\tfrac{x}{6}+\tfrac{y}{10}=1\Rightarrow 5x+3y=30\). Hence (A).
A line perpendicular to the x-axis is vertical, of the form \(x=\text{constant}.\) Through \((-2, 9)\) it is \(x=-2\), i.e. \(x+2=0.\) Hence (C).
Rewrite \(\dfrac{x}{10}-\dfrac{y}{4}=3\) as \(\dfrac{y}{4}=\dfrac{x}{10}-3\Rightarrow y=\tfrac{2}{5}x-12.\) Slope \(=\tfrac{2}{5}.\) Hence (C).
For \(4x-ay=8\): \(x\)-intercept \((y=0)\) is \(2\); \(y\)-intercept \((x=0)\) is \(-\tfrac{8}{a}.\) Condition \(-\tfrac{8}{a}=3(2)=6\Rightarrow a=-\tfrac{8}{6}=-\tfrac{4}{3}.\) Hence (D).
Let \(A=(p, 0),\ B=(0, q).\) Centroid of \(O, A, B\) is \(\left(\tfrac{p}{3}, \tfrac{q}{3}\right)=(1, 2)\Rightarrow p=3,\ q=6.\) Line: \(\dfrac{x}{3}+\dfrac{y}{6}=1\Rightarrow 2x+y=6.\) Hence (B).

Line \(3x+y=3\) has slope \(-3\), so a perpendicular has slope \(\tfrac{1}{3}.\) Through \((2, 2)\): \(y-2=\tfrac{1}{3}(x-2)\Rightarrow y=\tfrac{1}{3}x+\tfrac{4}{3}.\) The \(y\)-intercept is \(\tfrac{4}{3}.\) Hence (D).
Let intercepts be \(a\) and \(7-a\): \(\dfrac{x}{a}+\dfrac{y}{7-a}=1.\) Multiplying by \(a(7-a)\): \(x(7-a)+ya=a(7-a)\), so \(ya=(7-a)(a-x)\), i.e. \(ay=(7-a)(a-x).\) Hence (D).

Line \(2x+y=3\) has slope \(-2\); the perpendicular has slope \(\tfrac{1}{2}.\) Through \((1, 1)\): \(y-1=\tfrac{1}{2}(x-1)\Rightarrow y=\tfrac{1}{2}x+\tfrac{1}{2}.\) The \(y\)-intercept is \(\tfrac{1}{2}.\) Hence (D).

The incident ray \(x+\sqrt{3}y=\sqrt{3}\) has slope \(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) and meets the x-axis at \((\sqrt{3}, 0).\) On reflection in the x-axis the slope changes sign to \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), and the ray still passes through \((\sqrt{3}, 0)\): \(y=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-\sqrt{3})\Rightarrow\sqrt{3}y=x-\sqrt{3}.\) Hence (A).
Line 1: \(y=3x+c_1\) through \((30, 4)\Rightarrow c_1=4-90=-86.\) Line 2: \(y=6x+c_2\Rightarrow c_2=4-180=-176.\) Difference of \(y\)-intercepts \(=|-86-(-176)|=90.\) Hence (D).
If \(A(3, 4)\) bisects the intercept, the intercepts are \((6, 0)\) and \((0, 8).\) Line: \(\dfrac{x}{6}+\dfrac{y}{8}=1\Rightarrow 8x+6y=48\Rightarrow 4x+3y=24.\) Hence (B).

If \((\alpha, \beta)\) is the midpoint of the intercept segment, the intercepts are \((2\alpha, 0)\) and \((0, 2\beta).\) Line: \(\dfrac{x}{2\alpha}+\dfrac{y}{2\beta}=1\Rightarrow\dfrac{x}{\alpha}+\dfrac{y}{\beta}=2.\) Hence (C).
Midpoint \((1, 1)\) of the intercept segment gives intercepts \((2, 0)\) and \((0, 2).\) Line: \(\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{y}{2}=1\Rightarrow x+y=2.\) Hence (D).
Slope \(=\dfrac{2-1}{1-(-1/2)}=\dfrac{1}{3/2}=\tfrac{2}{3}.\) Line: \(y-2=\tfrac{2}{3}(x-1).\) At \(y=0\): \(-2=\tfrac{2}{3}(x-1)\Rightarrow x-1=-3\Rightarrow x=-2.\) Hence (A).
Line through \((1, 6)\) and \((3, -4)\) has slope \(\dfrac{-4-6}{3-1}=-5.\) Equation: \(y-6=-5(x-1)\Rightarrow y=-5x+11\Rightarrow 5x+y-11=0.\) Hence (A).
If \(P(1, 2)\) bisects the intercept, the intercepts are \((2, 0)\) and \((0, 4).\) Line: \(\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{y}{4}=1\Rightarrow 2x+y=4.\) Hence (D).

Write \(x\sec\theta+y\csc\theta=a\) as \(x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta=a\sin\theta\cos\theta\); its slope is \(-\tan\theta.\) The required perpendicular has slope \(\cot\theta=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}.\) Through \((a\cos^3\theta,\ a\sin^3\theta)\): multiplying by \(\sin\theta\) gives \(x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta=a\cos^4\theta-a\sin^4\theta=a(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)=a\cos 2\theta.\) Hence (B).

Slopes are \(m_1=3\) and \(m_2=\tfrac{1}{2}.\) Equal inclination to slope \(m\) gives \(\dfrac{3-m}{1+3m}=-\dfrac{1/2-m}{1+m/2}.\) Cross-multiplying and simplifying yields \(7m^2-2m-7=0\), so \(m=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4+196}}{14}=\dfrac{2\pm 10\sqrt{2}}{14}=\tfrac{1}{7}(1\pm 5\sqrt{2}).\) Hence (C).

The line through \((h, 0)\) and \((0, k)\) is \(\dfrac{x}{h}+\dfrac{y}{k}=1.\) Since \((3, 3)\) lies on it: \(\dfrac{3}{h}+\dfrac{3}{k}=1\Rightarrow\dfrac{1}{h}+\dfrac{1}{k}=\tfrac{1}{3}.\) Comparing with \(\dfrac{a}{h}+\dfrac{b}{k}=\tfrac{1}{3}\) gives \(a=1,\ b=1.\) Hence (C).

Midpoint of \(PQ\) is \(\left(\tfrac{1+k}{2}, \tfrac{7}{2}\right);\) slope of \(PQ=\dfrac{3-4}{k-1}=-\dfrac{1}{k-1}\), so the perpendicular bisector has slope \((k-1).\) Its \(y\)-intercept is \(\tfrac{7}{2}-(k-1)\cdot\tfrac{1+k}{2}=\dfrac{7-(k^2-1)}{2}=\dfrac{8-k^2}{2}.\) Setting this \(=-4\): \(8-k^2=-8\Rightarrow k^2=16\Rightarrow k=\pm 4.\) So \(k=-4\) is possible. Hence (A).

Line \(3x-2y=6\) has slope \(\tfrac{3}{2}\); the perpendicular has slope \(-\tfrac{2}{3}.\) With \(y\)-intercept \(2\): \(y=-\tfrac{2}{3}x+2.\) At \(y=0\): \(\tfrac{2}{3}x=2\Rightarrow x=3.\) Hence (D).
Midpoint \((4, -3)\) gives intercepts \((8, 0)\) and \((0, -6).\) Line: \(\dfrac{x}{8}+\dfrac{y}{-6}=1\Rightarrow 6x-8y=48\Rightarrow 3x-4y=24.\) Hence (C).

The dividing point in ratio \(1 : n\) is \(\left(\dfrac{n+2}{n+1}, \dfrac{3}{n+1}\right).\) The segment has slope \(3\), so the perpendicular has slope \(-\tfrac{1}{3}.\) Then \(3y-\dfrac{9}{n+1}=-\left(x-\dfrac{n+2}{n+1}\right)\), giving \(x+3y=\dfrac{9+(n+2)}{n+1}=\dfrac{n+11}{n+1}.\) Hence (A).

The mirror is \(7x-y+1=0\) (slope \(7\)) and the reflected ray is \(2x+y=1\) (slope \(-2\)), both through \((0, 1).\) Using equal angles of the incident and reflected rays with the mirror, the incident slope works out to \(\tfrac{41}{38}\), so the incident line through \((0, 1)\) is \(41x-38y+38=0.\) Hence (C).

Slopes are \(-\tfrac{2}{3}\) and \(-\tfrac{1}{k}.\) For perpendicularity \(\left(-\tfrac{2}{3}\right)\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{k}\right)=-1\Rightarrow\dfrac{2}{3k}=-1\Rightarrow k=-\tfrac{2}{3}.\) Hence (C).
Line \(y=3x-1\) has slope \(3\); the perpendicular has slope \(-\tfrac{1}{3}.\) Through \((1, 2)\): \(y-2=-\tfrac{1}{3}(x-1)\Rightarrow 3y-6=-x+1\Rightarrow x+3y-7=0.\) Hence (C).
Factor: \(x^3-yx^2+x-y=x^2(x-y)+(x-y)=(x-y)(x^2+1).\) Since \(x^2+1=0\) has no real solution, the real locus is \(x-y=0\), a single straight line. Hence (B).

Let intercepts be \(A(p, 0)\) and \(B(0, q).\) The point \((-4, 3)\) divides \(AB\) internally in \(5 : 3\): \(\left(\dfrac{3p}{8}, \dfrac{5q}{8}\right)=(-4, 3)\Rightarrow p=-\tfrac{32}{3},\ q=\tfrac{24}{5}.\) Line: \(\dfrac{x}{-32/3}+\dfrac{y}{24/5}=1\Rightarrow -9x+20y=96\Rightarrow 9x-20y+96=0.\) Hence (A).

Line \(2x+8y=10\Rightarrow x+4y=5\) has slope \(-\tfrac{1}{4}\); the perpendicular has slope \(4.\) Through \((5, 0)\): \(y=4(x-5)=4x-20.\) At \(x=0,\ y=-20\), so it meets the y-axis at \((0, -20).\) Hence (D).

From \(y+16=0\) and \(y=\alpha x\): \(\alpha x=-16\Rightarrow x=-\tfrac{16}{\alpha}.\) Concurrency with \(x=t+\alpha\) gives \(t=-\tfrac{16}{\alpha}-\alpha.\) Putting \(\alpha=-z\ (z>0)\): \(t=\dfrac{16}{z}+z\ge 2\sqrt{16}=8\) by AM-GM. The least positive value of \(t\) is \(8.\) Hence (D).

Slopes are \(m_1=-\sqrt{3}\) and \(m_2=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\) \(\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|=\left|\dfrac{-\sqrt{3}+1/\sqrt{3}}{1+1}\right|=\left|\dfrac{-2/\sqrt{3}}{2}\right|=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\) So \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}.\) Hence (A).

Perpendicular to \(3x-4y=6\) (slope \(\tfrac{3}{4}\)) has slope \(-\tfrac{4}{3}\), so write it as \(4x+3y=k.\) Intercepts \(\tfrac{k}{4}\) and \(\tfrac{k}{3}\) give area \(\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{k}{4}\cdot\dfrac{k}{3}=\dfrac{k^2}{24}=6\Rightarrow k^2=144\Rightarrow k=\pm 12.\) Thus \(4x+3y=12.\) Hence (A).
The required line is the perpendicular bisector of the given segment; computing the midpoint and the perpendicular slope gives \(3x+4y=1\). Hence (C).

Let the ratio be \(k : 1.\) The dividing point \(\left(\dfrac{6k-4}{k+1}, \dfrac{-5k+7}{k+1}\right)\) lies on \(2x+5y-7=0\): \(2(6k-4)+5(-5k+7)-7(k+1)=0\Rightarrow -20k+20=0\Rightarrow k=1.\) So the ratio is \(1 : 1.\) Hence (C).

Slopes: \(x+y=0\) has \(-1\); \(5x+y=4\) has \(-5\); \(x+5y=4\) has \(-\tfrac{1}{5}.\) The angle of \(x+y=0\) with \(5x+y=4\) gives \(\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{-1+5}{1+5}\right|=\tfrac{2}{3}\), and with \(x+5y=4\) gives \(\left|\dfrac{-1+1/5}{1+1/5}\right|=\tfrac{2}{3}\) as well. Two equal angles make the triangle isosceles. Hence (A).

Write \(3x+3y=-5.\) Dividing by \(\sqrt{3^2+3^2}=3\sqrt{2}\) and keeping \(p>0\): \(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}x-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}y=\tfrac{5}{3\sqrt{2}}\), so \(\cos\alpha=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\ \sin\alpha=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\) Then \(\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha=-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=-\sqrt{2}.\) Hence (C).

Since \(a, b, c\) are in A.P., \(2b=a+c\Rightarrow c=2b-a.\) Then \(ax+2by+c=0\) becomes \(a(x-1)+2b(y+1)=0\), which holds for all valid \(a, b\) precisely when \(x-1=0\) and \(y+1=0\), i.e. at the fixed point \((1, -1).\) Hence (A).

From \(x+y=3\) and \(y=3mx+1\): \(x+3mx+1=3\Rightarrow x(1+3m)=2\Rightarrow x=\frac{2}{1+3m}\). For \(x\) to be an integer, \((1+3m)\) must divide \(2\), so \(1+3m\in\{\pm1,\pm2\}\). Only \(1+3m=1\) (\(m=0\)) and \(1+3m=-2\) (\(m=-1\)) give integer \(m\). So there are \(2\) values. Hence (C).

Slopes: \(m_1=-\frac{2}{11}\) for \(2x+11y-7=0\) and \(m_2=-\frac{1}{3}\) for \(x+3y+5=0\). \(\tan\theta=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|=\left|\frac{-\frac{2}{11}+\frac{1}{3}}{1+\frac{2}{33}}\right|=\left|\frac{\frac{5}{33}}{\frac{35}{33}}\right|=\frac{1}{7}\). So \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{7}\). Hence (C).

The intercepts are \(x\)-intercept \(=-\frac{c}{a}\) and \(y\)-intercept \(=-\frac{c}{b}\). Area \(=\frac12\left|\frac{c}{a}\cdot\frac{c}{b}\right|=\frac{c^{2}}{2ab}=\frac{1}{32}\Rightarrow 16c^{2}=ab\), i.e. \((4c)^{2}=a\cdot b\). Thus \(a,\,4c,\,b\) are in G.P. Hence (D).

Let \(R=(x,y)\). Centroid \(=\left(\frac{2-2+x}{3},\frac{-3+1+y}{3}\right)=\left(\frac{x}{3},\frac{y-2}{3}\right)\). It lies on \(2X+3Y=1\): \(2\cdot\frac{x}{3}+3\cdot\frac{y-2}{3}=1\Rightarrow 2x+3(y-2)=3\Rightarrow 2x+3y=9\). Hence (A).
If \(ax+by+c=0\) passes through \((1,-2)\), then \(a-2b+c=0\Rightarrow a+c=2b\). This is the condition for \(a,\,b,\,c\) to be in A.P. Hence (B).
A line parallel to \(x-2y+8=0\) has the form \(x-2y+k=0\). Passing through \((0,4)\): \(0-8+k=0\Rightarrow k=8\). So the line is \(x-2y+8=0\). Hence (A).

\(px-qy=r\) meets the \(x\)-axis (\(y=0\)) at \(x=\frac{r}{p}\), so \(a=\frac{r}{p}\); it meets the \(y\)-axis (\(x=0\)) at \(y=-\frac{r}{q}\), so \(b=-\frac{r}{q}\). Therefore \(a+b=\frac{r}{p}-\frac{r}{q}=r\left(\frac{q-p}{pq}\right)\). Hence (B).

\(y=\sqrt{3}x\) and \(y=-\sqrt{3}x\) meet at the origin; with \(y=1\) the vertices are \((0,0),\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt3},1\right),\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt3},1\right)\). Each slant side has length \(\sqrt{\frac13+1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\) and the base \(=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\); all three sides are equal, so it is an equilateral triangle. Hence (A).

Line \(x+y=0\) has slope \(-1\). A line of slope \(m\) makes \(45^\circ\) with it when \(\left|\frac{m+1}{1-m}\right|=1\). This gives \(m=0\) (horizontal) or the vertical line. Through \((1,1)\) these are \(y-1=0\) and \(x-1=0\). Hence (D).

The diagonal \(7x-y+8=0\) has slope \(7\); the other diagonal is perpendicular, with slope \(-\frac17\), and passes through the vertex \((-4,5)\) (which does not lie on the first diagonal). So \(y-5=-\frac17(x+4)\Rightarrow 7y-35=-x-4\Rightarrow x+7y=31\), i.e. \(7y+x=31\). Hence (C).

Write the equation as \(a(x+y-1)+b(2x-3y+1)=0\). For it to hold for all \(a,b\): \(x+y-1=0\) and \(2x-3y+1=0\). Solving, \(x=\frac25,\ y=\frac35\). The fixed point is \(\left(\frac25,\frac35\right)\). Hence (D).

Centroid \(=\left(\frac{\cos\theta+\sin\theta}{3},\frac{\sin\theta-\cos\theta}{3}\right)\). On \(y=2x\): \(\sin\theta-\cos\theta=2(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)\Rightarrow -\sin\theta=3\cos\theta\Rightarrow\tan\theta=-3\). So \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(-3)\). Hence (C).

\(L\) is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining \((6,1)\) and \((-4,5)\). Midpoint \(=(1,3)\); slope of segment \(=\frac{5-1}{-4-6}=-\frac25\), so \(L\) has slope \(\frac52\). Through \((1,3)\): \(y-3=\frac52(x-1)\Rightarrow 2y-6=5x-5\Rightarrow 5x-2y+1=0\). Hence (C).

The nearest point is the foot of the perpendicular from \((3,-2)\). Along the normal direction \((1,1)\): \((3+t,-2+t)\) on \(x+y-3=0\Rightarrow (3+t)+(-2+t)-3=0\Rightarrow 2t-2=0\Rightarrow t=1\), giving \((4,-1)\). Hence (D).

A point on \(x+y+1=0\) is \((t,-1-t)\). Its distance from \(3x+4y+2=0\) is \(\frac{|3t+4(-1-t)+2|}{5}=\frac{|-t-2|}{5}=\frac15\Rightarrow |t+2|=1\Rightarrow t=-1\) or \(t=-3\), giving \((-1,0)\) and \((-3,2)\). Both options (B) and (D) satisfy the condition; the keyed answer is (B).

For \(x\sec\theta+y\,\mathrm{cosec}\,\theta=a\): \(p_1=\frac{a}{\sqrt{\sec^{2}\theta+\mathrm{cosec}^{2}\theta}}=a\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac{a}{2}\sin2\theta\), so \(4p_1^{2}=a^{2}\sin^{2}2\theta\). For \(x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta=a\cos2\theta\): \(p_2=|a\cos2\theta|\), so \(p_2^{2}=a^{2}\cos^{2}2\theta\). Hence \(4p_1^{2}+p_2^{2}=a^{2}(\sin^{2}2\theta+\cos^{2}2\theta)=a^{2}\). Hence (B).

Points at distance \(\sqrt5\) from \(x-2y+1=0\) lie on two lines parallel to it; points at distance \(\sqrt{13}\) from \(2x+3y-1=0\) lie on two lines parallel to it. The two pairs are non-parallel, so they intersect in \(2\times2=4\) points. Hence (C).

Rewrite \(6x+8y=15\) as \(3x+4y=\frac{15}{2}\). Distance between \(3x+4y=9\) and \(3x+4y=\frac{15}{2}\) is \(\frac{\left|9-\frac{15}{2}\right|}{\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}}=\frac{\frac{3}{2}}{5}=\frac{3}{10}\). Hence (A).

Slope through \((k,2k)\) and \((3k,3k)\) is \(\frac{3k-2k}{3k-k}=\frac12\). The line is \(y-2k=\frac12(x-k)\); using \((3,1)\): \(1-2k=\frac12(3-k)\Rightarrow 2-4k=3-k\Rightarrow k=-\frac13\). The line through \((3,1)\) with slope \(\frac12\) is \(x-2y-1=0\). Distance from origin \(=\frac{|-1|}{\sqrt{1+4}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}\). Hence (D).

Write \(\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1\) as \(bx+ay-ab=0\). Distance from origin \(=\frac{|ab|}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}=p\Rightarrow p^{2}=\frac{a^{2}b^{2}}{a^{2}+b^{2}}\Rightarrow\frac{1}{p^{2}}=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{a^{2}b^{2}}=\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}\). Hence (A).

For \(x\sec\theta+y\,\mathrm{cosec}\,\theta=a\): \(p=\frac{a}{\sqrt{\sec^{2}\theta+\mathrm{cosec}^{2}\theta}}=a\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac{a}{2}\sin2\theta\Rightarrow 4p^{2}=a^{2}\sin^{2}2\theta\). For \(x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta=a\cos2\theta\): \(q=|a\cos2\theta|\Rightarrow q^{2}=a^{2}\cos^{2}2\theta\). So \(4p^{2}+q^{2}=a^{2}(\sin^{2}2\theta+\cos^{2}2\theta)=a^{2}\). Hence (D).
Intercept form: \(\frac{x}{1/3}+\frac{y}{1/4}=1\Rightarrow 3x+4y=1\). Distance from origin \(=\frac{|{-1}|}{\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}}=\frac{1}{5}\). Hence (D).

The perpendicular has slope \(\frac34\), so \(\cos\alpha=\frac45,\ \sin\alpha=\frac35\). Normal form \(x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha=p\): \(\frac45x+\frac35y=\pm5\Rightarrow 4x+3y=\pm25\), i.e. \(4x+3y\pm25=0\). Hence (B).
A point on \(x+y=4\) is \((x,4-x)\). Distance from \(4x+3y-10=0\): \(\frac{|4x+3(4-x)-10|}{5}=\frac{|x+2|}{5}=1\Rightarrow x=3\) or \(x=-7\), giving \((3,1)\) and \((-7,11)\). Hence (A).

The greatest distance from \((-1,2)\) to a line through \((2,-3)\) is the distance between the two points: \(\sqrt{(2+1)^{2}+(-3-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{34}\approx5.83\). Since \(8>\sqrt{34}\), no line through \((2,-3)\) can be \(8\) units from \((-1,2)\). Number of lines \(=0\). Hence (D).
Slope of \(2x-3y+5=0\) is \(\frac23\); the perpendicular has slope \(-\frac32\). With \(y\)-intercept \(3\): \(y=-\frac32x+3\Rightarrow 2y=-3x+6\Rightarrow 3x+2y-6=0\). Hence (A).

A variable line whose signed distances from given points sum to zero passes through their centroid. Centroid of \((2,0),(0,2),(-2,-2)\) is \(\left(\frac{2+0-2}{3},\frac{0+2-2}{3}\right)=(0,0)\). Hence (B).

The perpendicular distance from the origin to \(L\) is unchanged by rotation of axes about the origin. With intercepts \(a,b\) this distance is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}}}\); with intercepts \(p,q\) it is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{p^{2}}+\frac{1}{q^{2}}}}\). Equating, \(\frac{1}{a^{2}}+\frac{1}{b^{2}}=\frac{1}{p^{2}}+\frac{1}{q^{2}}\). Hence (C).

\(L:\frac{x}{5}+\frac{y}{b}=1\) through \((13,32)\): \(\frac{13}{5}+\frac{32}{b}=1\Rightarrow\frac{32}{b}=-\frac{8}{5}\Rightarrow b=-20\). So \(L:4x-y=20\) (slope \(4\)). \(K\) parallel to \(L\): \(\frac{x}{c}+\frac{y}{3}=1\) has slope \(-\frac{3}{c}=4\Rightarrow c=-\frac34\), giving \(K:4x-y=-3\). Distance between \(4x-y-20=0\) and \(4x-y+3=0\) is \(\frac{|-20-3|}{\sqrt{4^{2}+1^{2}}}=\frac{23}{\sqrt{17}}\). Hence (D).
Along the normal \((1,1)\): \((2+t,4+t)\) on \(x+y=4\Rightarrow (2+t)+(4+t)=4\Rightarrow 2t=-2\Rightarrow t=-1\), giving foot \((1,3)\). Hence (A).
The line is \(y=mx+4\Rightarrow mx-y+4=0\). Distance from origin \(=\frac{|4|}{\sqrt{m^{2}+1}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{m^{2}+1}}\). Hence (C).
Along the normal \((1,1)\): \((t,t)\) on \(x+y=2\Rightarrow 2t=2\Rightarrow t=1\), giving foot \((1,1)\). Hence (C).

The constant term is \(-1\), so \(p=\frac{|-1|}{\sqrt{\left(\frac{\sin\alpha}{b}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\cos\alpha}{a}\right)^{2}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{\sin^{2}\alpha}{b^{2}}+\frac{\cos^{2}\alpha}{a^{2}}}}=\frac{|ab|}{\sqrt{a^{2}\sin^{2}\alpha+b^{2}\cos^{2}\alpha}}\). Hence (D).
Write the lines as \(x-y+a=0\) and \(x-y+b=0\). Distance \(=\frac{|a-b|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}}}=\frac{|a-b|}{\sqrt2}\). Hence (A).

The line is \(mx-y+\frac{a}{m}=0\). Foot of perpendicular from \((a,0)\) along normal \((m,-1)\): \((a+mt,\,-t)\) on the line gives \(m(a+mt)+t+\frac{a}{m}=0\Rightarrow (m^{2}+1)t=-a\frac{m^{2}+1}{m}\Rightarrow t=-\frac{a}{m}\). Foot \(=\left(a-a,\ \frac{a}{m}\right)=\left(0,\frac{a}{m}\right)\). Hence (A).
Intercept form: \(\frac{x}{3}+\frac{y}{4}=1\Rightarrow 4x+3y=12\). Distance from origin \(=\frac{12}{\sqrt{4^{2}+3^{2}}}=\frac{12}{5}\). Hence (D).

Along the normal \((2,1)\): \((3+2t,4+t)\) on \(2x+y-7=0\Rightarrow 2(3+2t)+(4+t)-7=0\Rightarrow 5t+3=0\Rightarrow t=-\frac35\). Foot \(=\left(3-\frac65,\ 4-\frac35\right)=\left(\frac95,\frac{17}{5}\right)\). Hence (A).

By symmetry, the intersection of \(\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1\) and \(\frac{x}{b}+\frac{y}{a}=1\) satisfies \(x=y\) (their sum/difference forces \((a-b)(x-y)=0\), and \(a\neq b\)). The line through the origin and this point is \(y=x\), i.e. \(y-x=0\). Hence (C).
The combined line is \((6+3\lambda)x+(-7-\lambda)y+(8+5\lambda)=0\). For it to be parallel to the \(y\)-axis, the coefficient of \(y\) must vanish: \(-7-\lambda=0\Rightarrow\lambda=-7\). Hence (A).

Intersection of \(x-2y=1\) and \(x+3y=2\): subtracting gives \(5y=1\Rightarrow y=\frac15,\ x=\frac75\). A line parallel to \(3x+4y=0\) is \(3x+4y+k=0\); through \(\left(\frac75,\frac15\right)\): \(\frac{21}{5}+\frac45+k=0\Rightarrow k=-5\). So \(3x+4y-5=0\). Hence (C).

Intersection of \(x+2y=4\) and \(2x+y=4\) is \(P=\left(\frac43,\frac43\right)\). A line through \(P\) cutting the axes at \((p,0),(0,q)\) satisfies \(\frac{4/3}{p}+\frac{4/3}{q}=1\). For midpoint \((h,k)\), \(p=2h,\ q=2k\), so \(\frac{2}{3h}+\frac{2}{3k}=1\Rightarrow 2(h+k)=3hk\). Locus: \(2(x+y)=3xy\). Hence (B).

From \(ax+2by+3b=0\) and \(bx-2ay-3a=0\), eliminate \(x\): the \(y\)-coordinate of intersection satisfies \(-(a^{2}+b^{2})(2y+3)=0\), so \(y=-\frac32\). The horizontal line is \(y=-\frac32\), i.e. below the \(x\)-axis at a distance \(\frac32\). Hence (D).

Solving \(100x+50y=1\) and \(75x+25y=-3\) gives \(x=-\frac{7}{50},\ y=\frac{15}{50}\). For equal intercepts \(\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{a}=1\): \(\frac{-7/50+15/50}{a}=1\Rightarrow a=\frac{8}{50}=\frac{4}{25}\). The line is \(x+y=\frac{4}{25}\Rightarrow 25x+25y-4=0\). Hence (C).
Dividing \(3a+2b+4c=0\) by \(4\): \(\frac34a+\frac12b+c=0\). Comparing with \(ax+by+c=0\) satisfied for all such \(a,b,c\), the fixed point is \(\left(\frac34,\frac12\right)\). Hence (C).

Median from \(O\) to midpoint of \(AB=(2,3)\): \(y=\frac32x\Rightarrow 3x-2y=0\). Altitude from \(O\) is perpendicular to \(AB\) (slope of \(AB=1\)), so slope \(-1\): \(x+y=0\). Joint equation \((3x-2y)(x+y)=3x^{2}+xy-2y^{2}=0\). Hence (D).

\(x+3y-9=0\) and \(2x-y-4=0\) meet at \((3,2)\). Concurrency requires \(4(3)+b(2)-2=0\Rightarrow b=-5\), so \((b,0)=(-5,0)\). Line through \((-5,0)\) and \((3,2)\) has slope \(\frac{2}{8}=\frac14\): \(y=\frac14(x+5)\Rightarrow 4y=x+5\Rightarrow x-4y+5=0\). Hence (D).

\(2y^2-xy-6x^2=0\) factors as \(y=2x\) and \(y=-\tfrac{3x}{2}\); with \(x+y=1\) the vertices are \(O(0,0)\), \(A(\tfrac13,\tfrac23)\), \(B(-2,3)\). The altitude from \(O\) (slope \(1\)) is \(y=x\); meeting the altitude from \(A\) gives the orthocentre \((\tfrac43,\tfrac43)\). Hence (A).

Lines \(x=5\) and \(y=3\) meet at \((5,3)\); their angle bisectors make \(45^\circ\): \((y-3)=\pm(x-5)\). Joint equation \([(x-5)-(y-3)][(x-5)+(y-3)]=(x-5)^{2}-(y-3)^{2}=0\Rightarrow x^{2}-y^{2}-10x+6y+16=0\). Hence (B).

The equation states that the sum of distances from \((2,0)\) and \((-2,0)\) equals \(4\), while the distance between these foci is also \(4\). Since the sum of focal distances equals the inter-focal distance, the ellipse degenerates to the segment joining the two foci (a degenerate conic, not a proper ellipse/circle/parabola). Hence (C).

Lines \(L_1:2x+3y-1=0\) and \(L_2:x+2y-1=0\) meet at \(C(-1,1)\); since \(O\) is the orthocentre, \(OC\perp L_3\), so \(L_3:ax+by-1=0\) has normal \((a,b)\parallel(1,-1)\Rightarrow b=-a\). The vertex \(A=L_2\cap L_3\) must satisfy \(OA\perp L_1\) (i.e. \(3A_x-2A_y=0\)); solving gives \(a=-8,\ b=8\). Hence (C).

On the line, \(y=4x-2\). Equidistant: \((x+5)^{2}+(y-6)^{2}=(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\Rightarrow 16x-8y+48=0\Rightarrow 2x-y+6=0\Rightarrow y=2x+6\). With \(y=4x-2\): \(4x-2=2x+6\Rightarrow x=4,\ y=14\). Point \((4,14)\). Hence (B).
Intercepts of \(5x+y=k\) are \(\frac{k}{5}\) and \(k\). Area \(=\frac12\cdot\frac{k}{5}\cdot k=\frac{k^{2}}{10}=10\Rightarrow k^{2}=100\Rightarrow k=\pm10\). Hence (B).

The triangle whose side-midpoints are \((0,1),(1,1),(1,0)\) has vertices \((0,0),(2,0),(0,2)\). Sides: opposite \((0,0)\) is \(2\sqrt2\); opposite \((2,0)\) is \(2\); opposite \((0,2)\) is \(2\). \(x\)-coordinate of incentre \(=\frac{2\sqrt2\cdot0+2\cdot2+2\cdot0}{2\sqrt2+2+2}=\frac{4}{2(\sqrt2+2)}=\frac{2}{2+\sqrt2}=2-\sqrt2\). Hence (A).

Intercepts of \(3\cos\theta\,x+4\sin\theta\,y=12\): \(\frac{12}{3\cos\theta}=\frac{4}{\cos\theta}\) and \(\frac{12}{4\sin\theta}=\frac{3}{\sin\theta}\). Area \(=\frac12\cdot\frac{4}{\cos\theta}\cdot\frac{3}{\sin\theta}=\frac{6}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}=\frac{12}{\sin2\theta}\). This is minimum when \(\sin2\theta=1\), giving area \(=12\). Hence (D).

Vertices: \(x=0\cap x-2y=1\Rightarrow\left(0,-\frac12\right)\); \(x=0\cap 2x+y-2=0\Rightarrow(0,2)\); \(x-2y=1\cap 2x+y-2=0\Rightarrow(1,0)\). The side \(x=0\) is vertical, so the altitude from \((1,0)\) is \(y=0\). Altitude from \(\left(0,-\frac12\right)\) perpendicular to the side of slope \(-2\) has slope \(\frac12\): \(y=\frac12x-\frac12\); meeting \(y=0\) at \(x=1\). Orthocentre \((1,0)\). Hence (B).

Interior integer points satisfy \(x\ge1,\ y\ge1,\ x+y\le20\). For each \(x=1,\dots,19\) there are \(20-x\) values of \(y\). Total \(=\sum_{x=1}^{19}(20-x)=\sum_{k=1}^{19}k=\frac{19\cdot20}{2}=190\). Hence (B).
Reflection in the line \(y=-x\) (i.e. \(x+y=0\)) maps \((x,y)\mapsto(-y,-x)\). So \((1,1)\mapsto(-1,-1)\). Hence (D).

From \(3x+4y=9\) and \(y=mx+1\): \(3x+4(mx+1)=9\Rightarrow x(3+4m)=5\Rightarrow x=\frac{5}{3+4m}\). For \(x\) integer, \((3+4m)\) divides \(5\): \(3+4m\in\{\pm1,\pm5\}\). Only \(3+4m=-1\) (\(m=-1\)) and \(3+4m=-5\) (\(m=-2\)) give integer \(m\). So \(2\) values. Hence (B).

\(xy=0\) gives the axes \(x=0\) and \(y=0\); with \(x+y=1\) the triangle has vertices \((0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\) with the right angle at \((0,0)\). For a right triangle the orthocentre is the right-angle vertex, \((0,0)\). Hence (A).

Vertices: \(3x-4y=0\cap5x+12y=0\Rightarrow(0,0)\); \(3x-4y=0\cap y=15\Rightarrow(20,15)\); \(5x+12y=0\cap y=15\Rightarrow(-36,15)\). Side lengths: opposite \((0,0)\) is \(56\); opposite \((20,15)\) is \(39\); opposite \((-36,15)\) is \(25\). Incentre \(x=\frac{56\cdot0+39\cdot20+25\cdot(-36)}{56+39+25}=\frac{-120}{120}=-1\), \(y=\frac{39\cdot15+25\cdot15}{120}=8\). Incentre \((-1,8)\). Hence (B).
Reflection in \(y+5=0\) (the line \(y=-5\)) keeps \(x\) and maps \(y\mapsto 2(-5)-y\). For \((-3,2)\): \(y'=-10-2=-12\), giving \((-3,-12)\). Hence (C).
\(xy=0\) gives the axes \(x=0\) and \(y=0\). With \(x=4\) and \(y=-5\) these bound a rectangle of width \(4\) and height \(5\). Area \(=4\times5=20\) sq. units. Hence (A).

Take a line through \((1,2)\) at angle \(\theta\): the point at distance \(r\) is \((1+r\cos\theta,2+r\sin\theta)\). On \(x+y=4\): \(3+r(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)=4\Rightarrow r=\frac{1}{\cos\theta+\sin\theta}\). With \(r=\frac{\sqrt6}{3}\): \(\cos\theta+\sin\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\Rightarrow\sqrt2\sin(\theta+45^\circ)=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\Rightarrow\sin(\theta+45^\circ)=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\). So \(\theta+45^\circ=60^\circ\) or \(120^\circ\), giving \(\theta=15^\circ\) or \(75^\circ\). Hence (B).
